clue.text: Shade southern bigwig wearing white

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for southern

indicators.note: whatever is worn has something else wrapped around it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: hock is a white wine from the Rhineland
a kingpin is the most important person in a group

explanation.surface: A colour named after a grandee from the South dressed all in white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'White' is not a colour here but a Rhine wine, and 'wearing' puts the bigwig inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Shocking pink is a vivid, intense hue of pink, made famous by Schiaparelli, so it is one particular shade.

clue.text: In Germany, she tours flipping tense place

indicators.note: to tour a place is to go all the way round it, so one piece encircles another

parts.note: sie is German for she

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taut means stretched tight, tense

explanation.surface: A German woman travels around a nerve-racking location.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tense' looks grammatical but is the adjective meaning tight; turned round, it sits inside the German pronoun, which spells SITUATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To situate something is to put it in a particular location or position, the verb sense of place.

clue.text: Rolling Stone inside of boat takes letter from Crete

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so one piece goes inside the other
the inside of a word is its middle, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the word

indicators.note: something rolling turns over, so its letters are read the other way

parts.note: a precious stone is a gem

explanation.surface: A member of the Rolling Stones is aboard a vessel, holding a letter mailed from a Greek island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolling Stone' reads as the band, but it splits: 'Rolling' turns the jewel round, and the middle of the boat wraps it.
explanation.definitionFit: Crete is Greek, and omega is the final character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a letter one might write there.

clue.text: Fool had dropped off novel

parts.note: to kid someone is to fool them
to drop off is to doze, so had dropped off is napped

explanation.surface: A jester nodded off over a book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fool' looks like a noun but is the verb; the two pieces name Robert Louis Stevenson's adventure story.
explanation.definitionFit: Kidnapped is the 1886 adventure book by Robert Louis Stevenson featuring David Balfour, an example of a novel.

clue.text: Kind of film I won't broadcast without adult

parts.note: a refusal: saying 'I won’t' is saying no

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: to air a programme is to broadcast it
A is the abbreviation for adult, as in film certificates

explanation.surface: Someone declares they won't screen a particular sort of movie unless a grown-up is present.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I won't' is a whole refusal giving NO; AIR loses its A to give IR.
explanation.definitionFit: Film noir is a genre of dark, cynical crime movies, so noir names a type of cinema.

clue.text: Tongue expert Olly got sacked after first of piercings

indicators.note: after places one piece behind the other in the answer
the first of a word is its opening letter alone

parts.note: the opening letter

indicators.note: a sacked town is ransacked and turned upside down, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A man called Olly who knows about tongues lost his job after getting a piercing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' suggests body piercings, but here it means a language.
explanation.definitionFit: A polyglot speaks or understands many languages, so is an expert in tongues in the linguistic sense.

clue.text: Sergeant perhaps seizing a Republican agent in NY

indicators.note: to seize is to grab hold, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: a sergeant is an example of a non-commissioned officer
taken as written
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A police sergeant arrests a Republican undercover operative in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' marks a sergeant as just one example of the abbreviation NCO.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang a narco or narc is an officer of a drug enforcement unit, hence an agent in New York.

clue.text: Institute entertaining Mike with ace meal

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to have them in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to institute something is to create it
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet
A is short for ace, as on playing cards

explanation.surface: A college hosts a man called Mike and offers a top-notch spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Institute' is a verb, not a college. A cream tea is a British afternoon snack of tea with scones, jam and clotted cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A cream tea is a light afternoon repast of scones, clotted cream, jam and a pot of tea.

clue.text: Cheery male bearing most of aerial attack

indicators.note: most of something is all but a little, so the final letter goes
bearing means carrying along, so one piece comes with the other

parts.note: a blitz is an aerial bombardment, cut short
he is the male pronoun

explanation.surface: A cheerful man carries most of the burden of an air raid.
explanation.walkthrough: BLITZ loses its last letter; HE follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: Blithe means happy, carefree and lighthearted, a near synonym for cheery.

clue.text: Boring grind to endlessly study utilitarianism?

indicators.note: without an end, a word loses its final letter

parts.note: the short word without its last letter
to read a subject is to study it at university
John Stuart Mill was the great champion of utilitarianism; the question mark signals the leap from doctrine to thinker

explanation.surface: Endless philosophy study described as tedious drudgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Read' is the British university sense of study a subject; the philosophy is replaced by its best-known exponent.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadmill is figuratively any tedious, repetitive routine of work from which there is no escape.

clue.text: Artist following game close to small country

indicators.note: following means coming after, so one piece is placed behind another

parts.note: RU is rugby union

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A painter tags along after a match somewhere near a tiny nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like a noun meaning nation, but it is the adjective, as in country life.
explanation.definitionFit: Country used as an adjective describes the countryside, away from towns, which is what rural means.

clue.text: Film Yugoslav at arcade screens

parts.note: runs across the word breaks

explanation.surface: A Yugoslav film is shown at an amusement arcade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screens' looks like it means showing a movie, but it is the concealment signal; the answer runs from yugoslAV AT ARcade.
explanation.definitionFit: Avatar is James Cameron's 2009 science fiction blockbuster, an example of a movie.

clue.text: Unaware of man in Sicily hiding second colonist

indicators.note: what is hidden is put out of sight, so that letter vanishes from the word

parts.note: signor is Italian for a man, Mister
S is the abbreviation for second
ants live in colonies

explanation.surface: A Sicilian gentleman secretly sheltering another settler, unaware.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiding' suggests holding inside, but here it means making the S disappear from SIGNOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ignorant of a fact lacks knowledge of it, so the adjective is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Break unwrapped supermarket mirror

indicators.note: with its wrapping removed, a word loses its outer letters

parts.note: Tesco, Britain's biggest grocery chain, minus its first and last letters
to ape someone is to copy or mirror them

explanation.surface: Someone smashes a mirror bought loose at the supermarket.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesco is a British supermarket chain. 'Mirror' is a verb, to imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: A break, as in a prison break, is a getaway from confinement, so the noun matches.

clue.text: Makes a racket when preparing rum colas

parts.note: the letters to be mixed

explanation.surface: A noisy bartender bangs about while making rum and cola cocktails.
explanation.walkthrough: The drinks being prepared are themselves the letters being mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: To clamour is to shout loudly and insistently, which is producing a din.

clue.text: Top dog cut piece of rolled meat

indicators.note: something cut is shortened, so the last letter is lopped off

parts.note: the top is number one, written NO I
a setter is a breed of gun dog, here cut short

explanation.surface: The leading hound bites off a portion of meat rolled up for cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top dog' reads as one phrase, but splits: the top is number one, abbreviated with a Roman numeral, and the dog is a setter missing its tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisette is a small round boneless cut of lamb, typically from the loin, rolled and tied.

clue.text: Most glum single maiden introduces Den

indicators.note: to introduce is to come before, so one piece leads the other

parts.note: sole means single, only
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
a den or nest is an animal's home

explanation.surface: A lonely young woman, very downcast, shows someone into her private room.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden over in cricket is one in which no runs are scored, written M on scorecards.
explanation.definitionFit: Solemn means serious and unsmiling, so its superlative describes the gravest, gloomiest person.

clue.text: Carp about hotel hound eating starter of red cabbage

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece surrounds another
what is eaten goes inside, so one piece swallows another

parts.note: koi are ornamental carp
Hotel is H in the NATO phonetic alphabet
short for labrador, a dog

indicators.note: the starter of a word is its first letter alone

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone moans about a hotel dog wolfing down red cabbage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Carp' looks like a verb meaning complain; it is the fish. R goes into LAB, and that goes with H into KOI.
explanation.definitionFit: Kohlrabi is a variety of cabbage grown for its swollen edible stem, sometimes called a cabbage turnip.

clue.text: Hidden access point cross constituent recalled

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters run back the other way

parts.note: a rood is a crucifix
a constituent is a part of a whole

explanation.surface: A secret entrance, remembered by an angry voter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' and 'constituent' look like an angry voter, but each is a noun; the pair is turned round whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A trapdoor is a flush, often concealed hatch in a floor or ceiling, so a secret way in.

clue.text: PM having run off before the French fight

indicators.note: before means placed in front, so one piece leads
something that has run off has gone away, so its letter disappears

parts.note: Liz Truss was briefly UK Prime Minister in 2022
R is the cricket abbreviation for run
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister flees ahead of a battle with France.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss's short premiership makes 'run off' doubly apt; the R leaves her name.
explanation.definitionFit: A tussle is a vigorous scuffle or struggle, a minor brawl.

clue.text: Places storing whiskey on area in any case

indicators.note: on means placed after, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area

indicators.note: to store is to keep inside, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to lay is to place, put down
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Shops stocking spirits locally, as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Places' is a verb, not a noun; it takes in the W and follows the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Always can mean regardless or at any rate, as in 'you can always ask', so it fits.

clue.text: Royal staff Peter's caught cavorting

indicators.note: cavorting is leaping about, so the letters jump into a new order

parts.note: the name with its possessive, used for its letters
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A palace employee named Peter is spotted frolicking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Royal staff' looks like courtiers, but staff is a rod; the 's makes Peter's give PETERS, and caught adds C.
explanation.definitionFit: A sceptre is the ornamental rod carried by a monarch as an emblem of sovereignty.

clue.text: OAP's shifting gold and half of loot in city

indicators.note: only half survives, so the rest of the word is dropped
shifting things move them about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: OAP is an old-age pensioner, with its possessive
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
a deletion: only the first half of the four-letter word survives

explanation.surface: A pensioner is moving gold and a share of stolen goods around a town.
explanation.walkthrough: An OAP is a British old-age pensioner. The answer is Brazil's largest metropolis.
explanation.definitionFit: São Paulo is the biggest Brazilian metropolis and one of the most populous urban areas in the world.

clue.text: Unclothed lads regularly poor on deck

parts.note: the word stripped of its first and last letters

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.walkthrough: 'On deck' sounds like a ship's position, but deck is the verb meaning decorate, and 'on' belongs to the letter run.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck something, as in deck the halls, is to decorate or embellish it.

clue.text: Run through essential ingredients of his yummy pasty

indicators.note: what is essential is at the heart, so only the central letters are kept

parts.note: the centre letter
the centre letter
a pasty complexion is a pale one

explanation.surface: Someone checks over the key components of a delicious Cornish pasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' looks like the British pastry (a pasty is a filled pastry turnover) but is the adjective for a pallid face.
explanation.definitionFit: To impale is to pierce with a sharp stake or spike, to skewer, which is to run a body through.

clue.text: Bitter that retired hombre carefully bottles

indicators.note: to retire is to withdraw, going backwards, so the letters are read from right to left
to bottle something is to keep it inside, so the phrase conceals a word

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bitter' tempts as beer, given 'bottles', but it is the adjective. BRECA is inside homBRE CArefully.

clue.text: Professor on board cycling to see group

indicators.note: riding round in a circle, letters move from the front to the back

explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a committee member, but it means a board game: Cluedo. Moving the P from front to back gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To lump things together is to put them into one batch, so the verb matches group.

clue.text: Broad and slow craft with learner at the bow?

parts.note: L is for learner, as on L-plates
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.walkthrough: L-plates mark a British learner driver. The question mark admits the whole clue paints a broad slow boat too.
explanation.definitionFit: Largo is a musical tempo marking meaning to play in a stately, broad and unhurried manner.

clue.text: Delight of two Americans covering Charlie in glue

parts.note: AM and US are both abbreviations for American

explanation.walkthrough: 'Covering' looks like a container, but covering the C hides it, so it vanishes from CEMENT.
explanation.definitionFit: Amusement and delight are both names for the pleasure or enjoyment felt at something entertaining.

clue.text: Certain data implicating officers near island sent west

to implicate is to involve or draw in, so one piece is wrapped around another

explanation.walkthrough: DI is a detective inspector in British police ranks.
